The client contacts one service entry point. The load balancer forwards the request to a selected backend, and that backend performs the application work. In the lesson's traced reverse-proxy example, the selected server reads from the database and returns the response through the balancer to the client. Clients need not choose an instance themselves. The deck does not name a ticketing /search or /purchase route; the path below is the proxy path it does trace.

Path-based routing to different server pools is Layer 7. L7 understands HTTP requests and can route different paths to different backend groups; the lesson's paths are /notes and /exports. It can also select a backend for each request, though rules that keep a user on one backend can override independent selection. L4 is the wrong unit for this split: it routes at the transport level and chooses a backend for a connection using network information, not HTTP paths.

Path routing needs readable HTTP contents. TLS encrypts the connection, so an HTTPS proxy normally terminates that TLS connection to inspect requests. Encryption onward to the backend is a separate configuration choice. The routing unit and this HTTP visibility are chosen before a balancing policy.

One reused L4 connection does not distribute its individual requests. L4 has already chosen the backend for that connection. Many requests can reuse the connection, they can all reach the same backend, and adding requests on that connection does not force new selections.

A balancer is unnecessary when one adequate server is enough because the service does not need traffic distribution or redundant serving. A balancer is not automatically useful in front of that server. Distribution can use spare capacity and support redundant serving, but the proxy adds a network hop and another component to operate.

evidence.quote: In this reverse-proxy example, the client contacts one service entry point. The balancer forwards the request to a selected backend. That server reads the note from the database and returns a response through the balancer to the client.
Clients need not choose an instance themselves. Distribution can use spare server capacity and support redundant serving, but the proxy adds a network hop and another component to operate.
One adequate server may be enough if the service does not need traffic distribution or redundant serving. A balancer is not automatically useful in front of it.
The backend performs the work; the balancer chooses where traffic goes.
Layer 4, or L4
Routes at the transport level. For TCP traffic, it typically chooses a backend for a connection using network information, not HTTP paths.
Many note requests can reuse that connection. They can all reach the same backend; adding requests on that connection does not force new selections.
Layer 7, or L7

Understands HTTP requests. It can route /notes and /exports to different backend groups, or select a backend for each request. Rules that keep a user on one backend can override independent selection.

Path routing requires readable HTTP contents. TLS encrypts the connection; an HTTPS proxy normally ends, or terminates, that TLS connection to inspect requests. Encryption to the backend is a separate configuration choice.
Choose the routing unit and required HTTP visibility before choosing a balancing policy.

Round robin takes turns across eligible backends. The count it uses is the turn: each request counts as one. It is a simple starting point for similar servers and similar work. These backends are not similar, and the work is not similar. A cheap seat lookup and a long request match the lesson's quick note read and slow export: they still each count as one request, so equal turns do not mean equal work. Round robin also does not use the fact that one backend is twice as capable as the other.

Least connections prefers the backend with fewer active connections. That connection count can help when connection durations vary, and the lesson says to consider least connections for long, uneven work. The limitation is that one connection may carry far more work than another, so the count can hide the difference between a cheap lookup and a long request.

Weights bias the share of traffic. For unequal capacity, a server with twice the measured capacity might start with twice the weight. The limitation is that configured weights are not a live measurement or a performance guarantee. No policy is universally best; actual latency and resource use have to be checked. The lesson's summary is to count requests or connections to select traffic, then measure the work those counts hide.

Another API backend alone may not raise throughput once the shared database is saturated. Balancing distributes existing capacity. More API servers can help when API processing is the bottleneck; they do not remove a saturated shared database bottleneck.

After one machine fails, the entry path and the surviving capacity both have to keep the service usable. One regional entry used for every request is a single point of failure. Clients need a reachable surviving path, such as another healthy zone, not merely another balancer that clients cannot reach, and that failover path has to be tested. Headroom is spare capacity. The survivors need enough capacity for the remaining load; otherwise redirecting traffic can overload them. Excess work is limited or rejected visibly instead of assuming redistribution solves it. Redundant components alone do not guarantee an available service. The lesson says to measure request latency, errors, and backend and database resource use under representative traffic, including a failure, and to verify both entry-path availability and surviving capacity.

Weights

A check that reflects readiness matters because readiness means the backend can accept useful new work. A health check only periodically probes a backend. The lesson's sample gap is this ticketing case: a process can answer /health while the handler cannot reach its required database. A health response of 200 can therefore appear while the purchase handler cannot use the database it needs. The check has to reflect the capabilities needed to serve the requests. A green check is a sample, not a promise.

Even a check aimed at those capabilities cannot detect every failure immediately. Checks have limited coverage, intervals, and failure thresholds. A backend can fail just after passing, and detection takes time.

Once the failure is detected and the backend is removed from eligible backends, it stops receiving new selections. That is what changes for new traffic. The lesson also says to check the product's all-unhealthy policy: some balancers send traffic to unhealthy targets when every target fails its checks, rather than refusing all traffic.

Removal cannot repair requests already underway. Those requests can still fail. Removal does not complete, undo, or safely replay them. Health-based routing reduces exposure to failure; it cannot guarantee every request succeeds.

evidence.quote: A green check is a sample, not a promise
A health check periodically probes a backend. Readiness means it can accept useful new work: a process can answer /health while the note handler cannot reach its required database.
Use a check that reflects the capabilities needed to serve notes. Checks have limited coverage, intervals and failure thresholds; a backend can fail just after passing. Detection takes time.
Once detected and removed from eligible backends, it stops receiving new selections. Requests already underway can still fail; removal does not complete, undo or safely replay them.
Check the product's all-unhealthy policy too. Some balancers send traffic to unhealthy targets when every target fails its checks, rather than refusing all traffic.
Health-based routing reduces exposure to failure; it cannot guarantee every request succeeds.

The cart is session state, information kept between a user's requests. If it lives only in server A's memory, B cannot read it. A later request that goes to B therefore cannot read the cart. If A fails, losing A can lose the only copy, so the cart can disappear with A.

Sticky routing, called affinity, prefers the same backend for that user's requests. It can keep ordinary requests on A. Its cost is that it skews load and restricts placement. It does not copy the session or preserve it when A fails. Stickiness does not copy the cart, and it does not guarantee that the cart survives A's failure.

Shared session storage lets either backend read the session, so B can read the cart and another server can read it if A is gone. Its cost is that it adds access or coordination work and a shared dependency whose availability matters too.

Routing a user consistently and making their state available on another server are separate responsibilities.

Drain A in this order: stop new connections, let open connections finish or hit the delay, then close them. Deregistering A makes the balancer stop creating new connections to A. Connection draining lets in-flight traffic finish on connections that are already open. The deregistration delay bounds that wait. The default is 300 seconds, and it can be changed.

New connection assignments stop when A is deregistered. The accepted 20-second request is already-accepted work, so stopping new connections does not stop it. The deck does not give a separate duration rule for 20 seconds. That request is in-flight work on an already open connection and can finish during the drain. Draining cannot promise zero interrupted work.

When the drain deadline expires, remaining connections can be closed. Closing them may interrupt an unfinished request. That work is not moved to B. The deck's steps end with that close; it does not describe a further shutdown action.

Merely stopping new L4 connections can still allow more HTTP requests on the reused client connection. If A stays healthy and an existing connection is not idle, the balancer can still send traffic, including further HTTP requests, on that connection. L4 chooses a backend for the connection. Many requests can reuse that connection and all reach the same backend; adding requests on that connection does not force new selections. Stopping new connections does not stop those requests.

Draining has to follow the routing unit. The drain has to manage the open connection's lifetime. A balancer that selects per HTTP request likewise has to manage requests it has already accepted.

evidence.quote: Many note requests can reuse that connection. They can all reach the same backend; adding requests on that connection does not force new selections.

During a deployment, deregistering A makes the balancer stop creating new connections to A. Connection draining lets in-flight traffic finish on connections that are already open. If A stays healthy and an existing connection is not idle, the balancer can still send traffic, including further HTTP requests, on that connection.

Stopping new connections does not stop those requests. The drain has to manage the open connection's lifetime. A balancer that selects per HTTP request likewise has to manage requests it has already accepted.

The deregistration delay bounds the wait. The default is 300 seconds, and you can change it. At the end of that delay, remaining connections can be closed. Closing them may interrupt an unfinished request. That work is not moved to B.
Stop new connections, let open connections finish or hit the delay, then close them. Draining cannot promise zero interrupted work.

The purchase transaction commits on A, and the response is lost. A committed write can remain stored even when the caller does not receive a response. The client cannot tell whether the write committed, so the timeout leaves the result uncertain. No response does not mean the saved purchase is absent.

A blind retry can create a duplicate because a blind retry on B can create a second note. The same gap applies to this purchase: B can create another purchase. The balancer does not make an arbitrary write idempotent. The application makes the effect safe to repeat.

Use the same idempotency key on every attempt: a stable ID for one logical operation. Deduplication means recognizing a repeat. All backends use a shared durable database record of the key and result, so the record is visible to B as well as A. Coordinate that record with the purchase in one transaction: insert a key that the database allows only once, create the purchase, and record its result; commit all or none. A repeat returns the recorded result without creating another purchase. Separate check-then-write steps can race or leave a crash gap, so those separate steps are not the coordination the lesson gives. The deck states the created record as a note; it does not use the word purchase.

A fresh key per retry, or a key remembered only in A's memory, cannot reliably protect a retry on B. The new key does not identify the same operation, and B cannot read a key stored only in A's memory.

Retries should have limits and delay during overload. Bound retry attempts and delay them, because extra requests consume capacity and can deepen overload. Retry policy does not replace duplicate protection or guarantee success.

evidence.quote: No response does not mean no saved note
A saves a new note, but its response is lost. The client cannot tell whether the write committed. A blind retry on B can create a second note.
Idempotency key

A stable ID for one logical operation, reused on every attempt. Deduplication means recognizing a repeat. A new key per retry, or a key remembered only in A's memory, cannot reliably protect a retry on B.

In one transaction, insert a key that the database allows only once, create the note and record its result; commit all or none. A repeat returns the recorded result without creating another note. Separate check-then-write steps can race or leave a crash gap.
